positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that for agentic GenAI devices, 'human oversight' may be asserted as a design claim without evidence that a real, present, uncoerced human actually authorized each consequential action, and that accuracy of outputs alone is an insufficient regulatory focus.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require agentic GenAI-enabled devices to produce verifiable, tamper-evident records demonstrating that an accountable human authorized each consequential action at the time it occurred, so authorization can be proven after the fact, rather than accepting oversight as a design claim.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on whether an accountable human actually authorized each consequential autonomous act, which concerns the delegation of decision authority to an agent rather than output accuracy.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It challenges nominal human-in-the-loop assumptions by asking for proof that oversight was real, present, and uncoerced in actual operation.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts FDA's focus on agentic devices but argues human oversight should not be accepted as a design claim. Instead, FDA should require verifiable, tamper-evident records proving an accountable, uncoerced human authorized each consequential action at the time it occurred.
positions.source_passage: My central recommendation: for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, "human oversight" should not be accepted as a design claim. It should be required as a verifiable, tamper-evident record that a real, present, uncoerced human authorized each consequential action at the moment it was taken. The regulatory question for an autonomous clinical agent is no longer only whether the output is accurate. It is whether an accountable human authorized this specific consequential act — and whether that can be proven afterward.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a risk framework keyed to clinical indication or model type would not differentiate agentic devices by what autonomous actions they can take, treating note drafting for clinician signature the same as order placement or record alteration.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add reversibility and consequence of autonomously executable actions as explicit dimensions in the risk framework for agentic devices, and scale acceptance criteria so that more consequential, less reversible autonomous actions require stronger evidence of contemporaneous human authorization at the point of action.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on how much authority an agent may exercise without a human and asks for evidence of contemporaneous human authorization proportionate to the consequence of the autonomous action.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: It distinguishes risk by actions such as placing orders or altering records, which are operational workflow actions rather than diagnostic output errors.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the risk framework but asks FDA to differentiate agentic devices by the reversibility and consequence of actions the agent can take autonomously, not only clinical indication or model type, with acceptance criteria requiring proportionately stronger evidence of contemporaneous human authorization.
positions.source_passage: I recommend the risk framework distinguish agentic devices by the reversibility and consequence of the actions the agent can take autonomously, not only by clinical indication or model type. An agent that drafts a note for clinician signature is a different risk object from one that can place an order or alter a record. Acceptance criteria should scale accordingly: the more consequential and less reversible the autonomous action, the stronger the required evidence of contemporaneous human authorization at the point of that action.

positions.stakeholder_concern: For agentic devices that can take consequential actions, the commenter is concerned that there may be no reliable way to establish who authorized a given action and whether that person was actually present and acting without coercion.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should consider requiring, in premarket submissions for agentic devices, a demonstration that the device generates a verifiable, tamper-evident authorization record for each class of consequential action it can take, documenting who authorized it and whether they were present and acting freely.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on verifying that a human actually delegated authority for each consequential agentic action, including whether the authorizer was present and acting freely.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The proposed tamper-evident record is aimed at attributing responsibility for actions taken by an autonomous device, which FDA's question does not address as an evidentiary requirement.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts FDA's attention to agentic devices but asks CDRH to go further by requiring premarket demonstration that the device creates verifiable, tamper-evident authorization records for each class of consequential action, showing who authorized it and whether they were present and acting freely.
positions.source_passage: For agentic devices, I recommend CDRH consider requiring, as part of the premarket submission, a demonstration that the device produces a verifiable, tamper-evident authorization record for each class of consequential action it can take — evidence that answers who authorized this, and whether they were actually present and acting freely.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that relying on identity verification (especially biometrics) to govern agentic actions confuses identity with authorization and creates a centralized biometric database that becomes a privacy liability and security target. They argue presence and authorization can be evidenced without collecting or storing biometric identifiers.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA's evaluation of agentic GenAI-enabled devices should require proof of authorization for the specific action taken, rather than proof of identity at login, and should avoid pushing sponsors toward additional biometric collection.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment focuses on whether an agentic device's individual actions are demonstrably authorized, a question of act-level delegated authority rather than user identification.
gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: It warns that adding biometric authentication creates a stored-identifier honeypot that is itself a privacy and security exposure, framing the control choice as a security risk.

positions.public_summary: Commenter urges that oversight of agentic GenAI devices verify authorization for each specific action rather than user identity at login, and warns that added biometric authentication creates a privacy and security liability without proving that a given act was authorized.
positions.source_passage: This is achievable without collecting or storing biometric identifiers; presence and authorization can be evidenced without building a biometric database that itself becomes a privacy liability and a security target. The reflex solution — "add more biometrics" — creates exactly the honeypot that data-minimization principles counsel against, and it does not actually prove authorization of a specific act. The evaluation should ask for proof of authorization at the action, not proof of identity at login. Identity is not authorization.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a required human confirmation or review step could be satisfied by something other than a genuine human, such as a deepfake or an AI agent impersonating the human reviewer.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that any human verification or confirmation checkpoint in an agentic GenAI-enabled device be resistant to spoofing, so that a deepfake or an AI agent cannot substitute for the human.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The passage raises the possibility that a human oversight step is effectively delegated to or usurped by an AI agent standing in for the person.
gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: It treats spoofing resistance of the human verification step as a safety-relevant design requirement rather than a purely security matter.

positions.public_summary: Commenter recommends that human confirmation checks in GenAI-enabled devices be designed to resist spoofing, so that a deepfake or an AI agent cannot substitute for the human reviewer. The passage does not state a broader position on FDA's approach.
positions.source_passage: The check should also be resistant to spoofing, so a deepfake or an AI agent cannot stand in for the human.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without tamper-evident records showing whether each consequential agentic action was authorized by a human, postmarket surveillance of agentic device behavior becomes reconstructive guesswork, impeding adverse-event investigation, root-cause analysis, and detection of patterns across deployed agent fleets.
positions.requested_fda_action: Include in postmarket expectations for agentic GenAI devices the retention and auditability of authorization evidence, scaled proportionately to the consequence of the actions the device performs.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on recording whether a human authorized each consequential agentic action, treating authorization evidence as a regulated artifact.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It frames auditable authorization records as what makes monitoring and pattern detection tractable across a fleet of deployed agents rather than a single instance.

positions.public_summary: Supports the proposed postmarket approaches but asks FDA to add a requirement that agentic devices retain tamper-evident, auditable records of human authorization (or its absence) for consequential actions, scaled to action consequence, to make surveillance and root-cause analysis feasible.
positions.source_passage: Authorization records of the kind described above are also the substrate for meaningful postmarket surveillance. If each consequential agentic action carries a tamper-evident record of its human authorization (or of its absence), then adverse-event investigation, root-cause analysis, and pattern detection across a fleet of deployed agents become tractable. Without such records, postmarket monitoring of agentic behavior is largely reconstructive guesswork. I recommend postmarket expectations for agentic devices include retention and auditability of authorization evidence proportionate to the consequence of the actions the device performs.

positions.stakeholder_concern: For consequential, irreversible agent actions, relying on the model behaving as instructed is insufficient; the commenter draws on positive-control practice in other high-consequence domains, where unforgeable authorization (and multi-person concurrence for the gravest actions) is required.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should treat verifiable authorization by an accountable human at the point of a consequential action as an operational control manufacturers can be required to demonstrate, with the system failing safe absent that authorization.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment centers on limiting what authority an autonomous agent may exercise without unforgeable, verifiable authorization by an accountable human.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: It focuses on harm from unauthorized or erroneous irreversible actions being executed, rather than on output accuracy, and asks for fail-safe behavior at the point of action.

positions.public_summary: Addressing agentic devices, the commenter accepts heightened oversight but asks CDRH to go further: for the narrow set of consequential, irreversible actions, require demonstrable verifiable authorization by an accountable human—potentially multi-person concurrence—with the system failing safe absent authorization.
positions.source_passage: In domains where an erroneous or unauthorized act cannot be undone, we do not rely on asking the system to behave; we require positive human control — unforgeable authorization and, for the gravest actions, concurrence by more than one accountable person. That principle translates directly to autonomous clinical agents: for the narrow set of actions consequential and irreversible enough to warrant it, no agent should be able to complete the action without verifiable authorization by an accountable human, and the system should fail safe in the absence of that authorization. I encourage CDRH to treat verifiable human authorization at the point of the consequential action as an operational control that manufacturers can be asked to demonstrate
